The UHC promise has three parts

01 · UNIVERSALITY

For all

Coverage is a population-wide goal, not a benefit limited to a selected group.

02 · ACCESS

Needed services

All people should be able to access the health services they need.

03 · PROTECTION

No financial hardship

Paying for care should not expose people to financial hardship.

WHO · Universal Health Coverage

An integrated definition of UHC

Access to key promotive, preventive, curative and rehabilitative health interventions for all at an affordable cost—thereby achieving equity in access.Lancet · 2006

PromotivePreventiveCurativeRehabilitative

How do we know when UHC is in place?

Criterion 1 · Legal entitlement

Legislation explicitly states that the entire population is covered by a defined health plan.

Criterion 2 · Service & insurance indicators

Access to at least skilled attendance at birth, alongside insurance coverage for 90% of the population.

WHO (2009) and ILO (2007)

Health Financing
8 / 48

Measurement of financial protection.

WHY OUT-OF-POCKET SPENDING MATTERS

Significant out-of-pocket health spending can harm well-being, especially for people who are poor.

Unpredictable
Serious illness can create major economic risk for families.
Predictable
The routine costs of primary care—including medicines—can also be a serious burden.
CATASTROPHIC HEALTH EXPENDITURE

Out-of-pocket payment for health exceeds a specified share of household income, expenditure, or capacity to pay.

10%
OF TOTAL HOUSEHOLD EXPENDITURE

One traditional SDG 3.8.2 threshold for identifying catastrophic out-of-pocket health spending.

WHO also reports a 25% budget-share threshold; its 2025 revision uses 40% of discretionary household budget.
Source: WHO SDG 3.8.2 indicator definitions ↗

Health financing functions and objectives

COLLECTING
Sufficient and sustainable revenue
Provide social health protection for all.
POOLING
Equitable and efficient risk sharing
Manage collected revenues to pool health risks fairly.
PURCHASING
The right services and incentives
Purchase services strategically from public and private providers.

The design question is not only how much money enters the system, but how it is shared and spent.

Provider payment basics

DEFINITION

Method(s) used to allocate resources to the point of service (POS).

PURPOSE

Deliberately create behavioral incentives for providers to achieve priority practice-pattern objectives.

PRINCIPLES OF PAYMENT POLICY
EFFICIENCY

Achieve the most health benefits from a fixed supply of resources.

EQUITY

Pay more to those who do more.

ACCESS

Promote equal access for all, regardless of location or severity.

ASSUMPTIONProfit maximization
Payment methods shape provider incentives

HOW

Set payment methods and incentives.

The source frames purchasing as strategic, allocatively efficient, and technically efficient.

Financing · 27
Health Financing
28 / 48

Common payment mechanisms

Payment methodDefinition
Line-item budgetProviders receive a fixed amount to cover specific input expenses (e.g., personnel, drugs, utilities).
Global budgetProviders receive a fixed amount for a set period to cover aggregate expenditures. The budget is flexible and not tied to line items.
Per diemHospitals are paid a fixed amount per day for each admitted patient treated.
Case-based (DRG)Hospitals are paid a fixed amount per admission, based on patient and clinical characteristics.
Fee for serviceProviders are paid for each individual service. Fees are fixed in advance.
Per capita (capitation)Providers receive a fixed amount in advance to provide a defined set of services for each enrolled individual over a fixed period.
Payment methods allocate resources and shape incentives

29 / 48

Moving from passive to strategic purchasing

PASSIVE PURCHASING

Allocation by norms

  • Resource allocation using norms
  • Little or no selectivity of providers
  • Little or no quality monitoring
  • Price and quality taker
STRATEGIC PURCHASING

Deliberate incentives

  • Payment systems that create deliberate incentives
  • Selective contracting
  • Quality improvement and rewards
  • Price and quality maker
Purchasing design shapes provider incentives and accountability

35 / 48

What have we learned so far?

01 · SHARE RISK

Pooling is essential

Risk pooling supports equity and financial risk protection.

02 · INTEGRATE

Fewer, broader pools

More integrated pools can improve redistribution.

03 · PROTECT

Limit OOP dependence

Heavy reliance on out-of-pocket payments and voluntary private insurance will not achieve UHC.

04 · PRIORITIZE

Use limited resources well

Government funds are limited; choose who and what to cover, then spend effectively.

Key takeaways

Policy choices · 39
Health Financing
40 / 48

Raise and prioritize domestic revenue

01 · BUDGET

Give health greater priority

Increase the priority of health in budget allocations.

02 · DOMESTIC

Raise more domestically

Build a larger domestic contribution to health financing.

03 · TAX

Use broad and earmarked taxes

Such as sales taxes and “sin taxes,” particularly alcohol and tobacco.

04 · SOLIDARITY

Consider solidarity levies

Such as small fees on airline tickets or financial transactions.

Where inefficiency can arise

WORKFORCE

Costly or inappropriate staff mix; low motivation.

CARE DELIVERY

Unnecessary admissions/long stays; underused hospitals; errors and suboptimal quality; excess equipment, tests, and procedures.

LEAKAGE

Waste, corruption, and fraud.

INTERVENTIONS

Inefficient mix or inappropriate level of strategies.

MEDICINES

Underuse of generics; substandard/counterfeit drugs; inappropriate or ineffective use.

Monitor & report

Efficiency means getting more health from the resources already available.

Policy choices · 44
Health Financing
45 / 48

Three roads to universal coverage

UNITED KINGDOM

Single-payer coverage

WHAT

Comprehensive care; no co-pay at point of service.

WHO

All residents.

FINANCING & DELIVERY

Government finances through taxes and pays providers directly.

THE NETHERLANDS

Regulated private coverage

WHAT

Government-defined benefits; deductibles for some services.

WHO

Everyone required to have insurance, subject to exceptions.

FINANCING & DELIVERY

Regulated private insurance; insurers pay providers.

FRANCE

Mixed public-private coverage

WHAT

Wide service range with some cost-sharing.

WHO

All residents.

FINANCING & DELIVERY

Government finances nonprofit funds; many people add private insurance.

Redrawn from Seervai, Shah & Osborn, “How Other Countries Achieve Universal Coverage,” The Commonwealth Fund, 2017.

Commonwealth Fund figure
Country pathways · 45
Health Financing
46 / 48

Different paths.
One population-wide goal.

01 · EXTEND

Reach the whole population

Include people who are hardest to reach.

02 · FINANCE

Make enough resources available

Build funding that can support covered services.

03 · STEWARD

Prevent avoidable waste

Use resources effectively and maintain political commitment.

Countries take different paths. The test is whether each path improves access, equity, and protection for the population.

Investigate your country’s health financing

YOUR TASK · USE THE WHO GLOBAL HEALTH EXPENDITURE DATABASE
01

Choose the country you are from

Open the GHED Data Explorer or country visualisations.

02

Focus on 2023

Use 2023 for each indicator where available. If a value is missing, use the most recent earlier year and label it clearly; do not silently mix years.

03

Measure spending

Record current health expenditure per capita (US$) and current health expenditure as a share of GDP.

04

Trace who pays

Describe the financing mix: government, households/out-of-pocket, external sources, and compulsory or voluntary arrangements where reported.

SHARE BACK

Three findings

  1. How much is spent?
  2. Which sources finance it?
  3. What stands out about the mix?
